about_dish.full: Sogalbi jjim is Korea's celebration braise — beef short ribs simmered for hours in a sweet-savory soy sauce until the meat surrenders off the bone. The secret is the double boil: parboil first to purge impurities, then a long, patient simmer with radish, carrot, and mushrooms soaking up the glossy sauce.

mistakes: Skipping the parboil. Boiling the ribs once and rinsing them clean is what keeps the braising liquid clear and free of any gamey taste — skip it and there's no fixing the broth later.
Adding all the vegetables at once. Radish needs 15 minutes, carrot and mushrooms 10, onion only 5 — stagger them so nothing turns to mush.
Skipping the rest. Those 10 minutes covered off the heat let the sauce settle into the meat. Serve it straight off the boil and it tastes flat by comparison.

steps.text: Rinse the short ribs clean in cold water.
Place the rinsed ribs in a large pot, pour in enough water to cover them, and bring to a boil.
Once boiling, lift the ribs out and rinse them again thoroughly under running water.
Drain the rinsed ribs in a colander and shake off the excess water.
Make the braising sauce: combine the chopped green onion, soy sauce, brown sugar, cooking wine, water, garlic, ginger, pepper, and sesame oil in a bowl. Stir until the sugar is fully dissolved.
Put the drained ribs and the braising sauce in the large pot, then pour in 1 liter of water.
Bring the pot to a boil over high heat and cook for 1 hour.

While it boils, prep the vegetables: cut the radish into flat squares (nabak), cut the carrot into generous 5 cm chunks, cut the mushrooms into large bite-size pieces, and cut the onion into 3–5 cm chunks.
As it boils, skim off the foam and impurities that rise to the surface with a spoon.
After 1 hour, add the radish and cook for 15 minutes.
Add the carrot and cook for 10 minutes.
Add the mushrooms and cook for 10 minutes.
Add the onion and cook for 5 more minutes.
When the onion turns translucent, add the peppers and green onion, cook for 3 minutes, then turn off the heat.
Cover with the lid and let it rest for 10 minutes before serving.

en.story: Sogalbi jjim is what my family makes when everyone comes home — the pot alone is the centerpiece. The first time I made it, I skipped the parboil to save time, and the broth turned cloudy with a gamey edge I couldn't fix. Now I never skip it: boil once, rinse clean, and the second simmer rewards you with a clear, glossy sauce and meat that falls off the bone.
